scope: Add whole-word masking, SpanBERT/SBO and ALBERT SOP to the existing BERT explanation in the original English language, shared unchanged by both locales. This reversible journal preserves prior acceptance revisions; it is not itself content acceptance.

changes.old: ## DeBERTa: разделить содержание и относительное положение
changes.new: ## Whole-word masking selects targets together If a name is tokenized as `phil ##am ##mon`, predicting only `##am` leaves the other parts visible. Whole-word masking groups those three positions when selecting prediction targets. It keeps WordPiece tokenization and the same vocabulary-sized prediction head; it does not turn the name into one new vocabulary item. The original BERT release explains the unchanged prediction task: > The training is identical -- we still predict each masked WordPiece token > independently. The improvement comes from the fact that the original prediction > task was too 'easy' for words that had been split into multiple WordPieces. — Google Research, [BERT README, Whole Word Masking Models, May 31, 2019](https://github.com/google-research/bert/blob/eedf5716ce1268e56f0a50264a88cafad334ac61/README.md#L74-L118), Apache-2.0. This is the authors' motivation, not a claim that every partially visible word has only one possible completion. In the pinned generator, a piece beginning with `##` joins the preceding candidate group. The groups are shuffled, then selected under the prediction budget. A group that would exceed the remaining budget is skipped rather than partly selected. Consequently, grouping can leave a budget underfilled; selecting exactly 15% of the positions in every short example is not a requirement. The following reduced selector receives an explicit group order instead of drawing a random shuffle. It isolates grouping and budget handling from token replacement: ```python def whole_word_groups(pieces): groups = [] for index, piece in enumerate(pieces): if piece in ("[CLS]", "[SEP]"): continue if piece.startswith("##") and groups: groups[-1].append(index) else: groups.append([index]) return groups def choose_word_targets(pieces, group_order, budget): groups = whole_word_groups(pieces) chosen = [] for group_index in group_order: candidate = groups[group_index] if len(chosen) + len(candidate) <= budget: chosen.extend(candidate) return sorted(chosen) pieces = ["[CLS]", "the", "man", "likes", "play", "##ing", "[SEP]"] assert whole_word_groups(pieces) == [[1], [2], [3], [4, 5]] order = [3, 1, 0, 2] assert choose_word_targets(pieces, order, budget=2) == [4, 5] assert choose_word_targets(pieces, order, budget=1) == [2] assert choose_word_targets(["[CLS]", "play", "##ing", "[SEP]"], [0], budget=1) == [] targets = choose_word_targets(pieces, order, budget=2) corrupted = pieces.copy() corrupted[4] = "[MASK]" # An unchanged draw is allowed for the other selected piece. assert corrupted[5] == "##ing" assert [pieces[i] for i in targets] == ["play", "##ing"] ``` Both selected positions retain their original labels, even though one input piece is unchanged. The actual BERT generator applies its 80/10/10 replacement decision separately inside the selected group. Thus “select the whole word” does not mean “all its input pieces must be literal `[MASK]` tokens.” The README's all-MASK example illustrates one outcome, while [the generator, lines 341–415](https://github.com/google-research/bert/blob/eedf5716ce1268e56f0a50264a88cafad334ac61/create_pretraining_data.py#L341-L415) defines the replacement procedure. This code assumes a valid WordPiece sequence and a permutation of its candidate groups. Other tokenizers need their own word-boundary mapping; a SentencePiece boundary marker is not the same convention as `##`. The existing MLM head still predicts each selected subword separately from its contextual state. Whole-word selection changes the corruption distribution, not the encoder architecture or the attention visibility mask. The original release reports improved SQuAD and MultiNLI results for its new BERT-Large checkpoints. That does not establish a universal gain: [SpanBERT, Table 6](https://aclanthology.org/2020.tacl-1.5/) reports 77.7 coreference F1 for subword masking and 76.6 for whole-word masking in its particular bi-sequence ablation. Dataset, training budget, and the other objectives belong with any such comparison. ## SpanBERT: predict a span from its boundaries An extractive QA model locates a contiguous answer, and a coreference model compares mentions such as `the champion` and `Denver Broncos`. Their downstream classifiers often read a span's boundary states. SpanBERT adds a pretraining loss that asks those states to retain enough information to predict the words between them. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/bert-objectives-2026-10-29/spanbert-boundary-objective.png|Original SpanBERT span-boundary objective and token predictions]] *Mandar Joshi, Danqi Chen, Yinhan Liu, Daniel S. Weld, Luke Zettlemoyer and Omer Levy, [SpanBERT, Figure 1, printed p. 65](https://aclanthology.org/2020.tacl-1.5.pdf#page=2). Original figure and complete caption, CC BY 4.0. Only outer page material was cropped; the formula, all token states and all arrows are retained.* The paper describes the auxiliary prediction directly: > Given a masked span of tokens > $(x_s,\ldots,x_e)\in Y$, where $(s,e)$ indicates its start > and end positions, we represent each token $x_i$ > in the span using the output encodings of the > external boundary tokens $\mathbf{x}_{s-1}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{e+1}$, as well > as the position embedding of the target token > $\mathbf{p}_{i-s+1}$: $$ y_i=f(h_{s-1},h_{e+1},p_{i-s+1}). $$ — [Joshi et al., section 3.2](https://aclanthology.org/2020.tacl-1.5/), CC BY 4.0. Bold contextual vectors in the source equation are written as $h$ here to distinguish them from input token IDs. In Figure 1, positions 5–8 contain `an American football game`. The external boundary states are $h_4$ for `was` and $h_9$ for `to`. To predict `football` at position 7, the boundary head receives $[h_4;h_9;p_3]$. It does not read $h_7$ directly. The ordinary MLM head does read $h_7$, so the same target has two prediction paths. The offset embedding distinguishes the first, second, third and fourth outputs for one common pair of boundaries. Without an offset or another position-dependent input, a deterministic head receiving the same two vectors would return the same vocabulary distribution at every position of the span. The offset specifies a location; the target word itself remains a label outside the input. The paper uses two dense transformations, each followed by GELU and LayerNorm: $$ \begin{aligned} u_i&=[h_{s-1};h_{e+1};p_{i-s+1}],\\ a_i&=\operatorname{LN}(\operatorname{GELU}(W_1u_i)),\\ y_i&=\operatorname{LN}(\operatorname{GELU}(W_2a_i)). \end{aligned} $$ The input vocabulary embedding matrix supplies the tied output weights for both predictions. For each selected token, the objective adds $$ L_i=-\log P_{\mathrm{MLM}}(x_i\mid h_i) -\log P_{\mathrm{SBO}}(x_i\mid y_i). $$ For illustrative probabilities 0.5 from MLM and 0.25 from SBO, this token contributes $-\log0.5-\log0.25=\log8\approx2.0794$. Dropping the second term would remove the training signal to the boundary head. The predictions within the span are not fed to one another as decoder inputs; this remains encoder pretraining, not autoregressive generation of the missing phrase. The small module below checks the two read paths. It starts with supplied final encoder states rather than running another Transformer. Its widths are 4 for a state and 2 for an offset, not the original model dimensions. ```python import math import torch from torch import nn import torch.nn.functional as F torch.manual_seed(131) dtype = torch.float64 final_states = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(12, 4, dtype=dtype)) offsets = nn.Embedding(4, 2, dtype=dtype) vocabulary = nn.Embedding(12, 4, dtype=dtype) boundary_head = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(10, 8, bias=False, dtype=dtype), nn.GELU(), nn.LayerNorm(8, dtype=dtype), nn.Linear(8, 4, bias=False, dtype=dtype), nn.GELU(), nn.LayerNorm(4, dtype=dtype), ) # Zero-based rows 3 and 8 are h_4 and h_9 in the original figure. boundary_inputs = torch.cat([ final_states[3].expand(4, -1), final_states[8].expand(4, -1), offsets(torch.arange(4)), ], dim=-1) sbo_states = boundary_head(boundary_inputs) sbo_logits = F.linear(sbo_states, vocabulary.weight) mlm_logits = F.linear(final_states[4:8], vocabulary.weight) span_targets = torch.tensor([4, 5, 6, 7]) sbo_loss = F.cross_entropy(sbo_logits, span_targets) mlm_loss = F.cross_entropy(mlm_logits, span_targets) direct_sbo_gradient, = torch.autograd.grad( sbo_loss, final_states, retain_graph=True ) assert direct_sbo_gradient[3].norm() > 0 assert direct_sbo_gradient[8].norm() > 0 assert torch.count_nonzero(direct_sbo_gradient[4:8]) == 0 same_offset_inputs = boundary_inputs.clone() same_offset_inputs[:, -2:] = boundary_inputs[0, -2:] same_offset_logits = F.linear( boundary_head(same_offset_inputs), vocabulary.weight ) torch.testing.assert_close( same_offset_logits, same_offset_logits[0].expand_as(same_offset_logits) ) (mlm_loss + sbo_loss).backward() assert final_states.grad[4:8].norm() > 0 assert offsets.weight.grad.norm() > 0 assert vocabulary.weight.grad.norm() > 0 assert math.isclose(-math.log(.5) - math.log(.25), math.log(8)) ``` The zero internal-state derivative above concerns direct inputs to the SBO head at the final encoder output. In a complete encoder, the boundary states themselves depend on other positions through attention. SBO can therefore backpropagate through those earlier dependencies. The check does not say that all internal-position computations receive zero gradient throughout SpanBERT. ### Sampling several words without introducing a decoder Whole-word masking can select isolated words. SpanBERT instead starts from a word boundary and extends a contiguous span. Its proposed length distribution favors short spans but includes lengths up to ten words; the total target budget is about 15% of subword positions. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/bert-objectives-2026-10-29/spanbert-span-lengths.png|Original SpanBERT distribution of sampled span lengths]] *Joshi et al., [Figure 2, printed p. 66](https://aclanthology.org/2020.tacl-1.5.pdf#page=3), CC BY 4.0. Complete original plot and caption. The horizontal axis counts words, not WordPiece positions or decoder tokens.* In the released implementation, weights $0.2(0.8)^{\ell-1}$ for $\ell=1,\ldots,10$ are normalized over that finite range: $$ P(\ell)=\frac{0.2(0.8)^{\ell-1}}{1-0.8^{10}}, \qquad \ell\in\{1,\ldots,10\}. $$ This produces mean length about 3.8, as in the paper. Sampling an unbounded geometric variable and replacing every value above ten by ten would instead accumulate a tail probability at ten. That is a different distribution from the plotted and implemented one. ```python import math weights = [.2 * .8**(length - 1) for length in range(1, 11)] length_probabilities = [weight / sum(weights) for weight in weights] mean_words = sum(length * probability for length, probability in zip(range(1, 11), length_probabilities)) assert math.isclose(sum(length_probabilities), 1.) assert 3.79 < mean_words < 3.80 clamped_geometric_mean = sum(.8**step for step in range(10)) assert 4.46 < clamped_geometric_mean < 4.47 assert not math.isclose(mean_words, clamped_geometric_mean) ``` See [the pinned sampling code, lines 74–132](https://github.com/facebookresearch/SpanBERT/blob/0670d8b6a38f6714b85ea7a033f16bd8cc162676/pretraining/fairseq/data/masking.py#L74-L132). The paper describes spans of whole words; the released loop also stops at the exact subword budget, so its final selected word can be cut short. The sampled length distribution does not imply that every realized span has that many complete words after budget and document boundaries are applied. The original span-level replacement setting draws the corruption type once for a span: MASK, random replacements, or unchanged text. This differs from BERT's per-piece replacement loop. Adjacent selected intervals can also merge before SBO boundary targets are prepared. External boundaries must exist; the implementation does not fabricate a context token outside the document. The model also uses a single contiguous training segment without NSP. That input change and the auxiliary objective must be separated when reading results. In the paper's 1.2M-step ablation, Table 7 reports: | Span-masking setting | SQuAD 2.0 Dev F1 | NewsQA Dev F1 | Coreference F1 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | two segments + NSP | 85.4 | 73.0 | 76.4 | | one segment | 86.7 | 73.4 | 76.3 | | one segment + SBO | 86.8 | 74.1 | 79.0 | The first transition changes both the segment construction and NSP. The second keeps single-segment span masking and adds SBO. Its coreference gain is much larger than its SQuAD gain in this ablation. These are not the final 2.4M-step test results, and they do not establish one fixed improvement from adding SBO to any model. In [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/06 Encoder, Decoder и Encoder-Decoder/07 T5 — text-to-text Transformer|T5]], a deleted span is replaced by one sentinel and a separate causal decoder generates the missing text. SpanBERT retains the corrupted sequence's positions and predicts its selected tokens through encoder heads. The two methods share span-based corruption, but their target format, conditional dependencies and computation are different. ## ALBERT: classify the order of two document segments NSP's negative example can combine a paragraph about unlocking a door with a paragraph about penguins. A classifier can use the change of topic without learning which of two related events came first. ALBERT's sentence-order prediction (SOP) changes how the negative pair is built. Take consecutive segments from one document: | Label | First segment | Second segment | |---|---|---| | ordered | She unlocked the door. | Then she entered. | | swapped | Then she entered. | She unlocked the door. | Both rows contain the same words. A topic histogram of the combined text is identical, so that feature alone cannot distinguish these two labels. Token order, positions and segment membership do change. The segments need not be single linguistic sentences. The released ALBERT generator implements the swapped case as follows: ```python title="Original ALBERT pair swap — Apache-2.0" elif not FLAGS.random_next_sentence and rng.random() < 0.5: is_random_next = True for j in range(a_end, len(current_chunk)): tokens_b.extend(current_chunk[j]) # Note(mingdachen): in this case, we just swap tokens_a and tokens_b tokens_a, tokens_b = tokens_b, tokens_a ``` — Google Research, [create_pretraining_data.py, lines 338–343](https://github.com/google-research/albert/blob/b772393d3dae115b493258ce8e37c17b2cc62100/create_pretraining_data.py#L338-L343), Copyright 2019 The Google Research Authors, Apache-2.0. The historical variable name `is_random_next` also marks a swapped SOP pair; it does not mean that this branch sampled another document. Input assembly still produces `[CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP]`. The first segment and its initial special tokens receive type 0, the second segment and final separator type 1. Positional IDs run through the assembled sequence. The binary head reads the pooled `[CLS]` state, and its cross-entropy is added to MLM loss. The following calculation uses supplied logits to check target labels, mean cross-entropy and its gradient: ```python from collections import Counter import math import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def assemble_sop(first, second): tokens = ["[CLS]", *first, "[SEP]", *second, "[SEP]"] types = [0] * (len(first) + 2) + [1] * (len(second) + 1) return tokens, types first = ["she", "unlocked", "the", "door", "."] second = ["then", "she", "entered", "."] ordered, ordered_types = assemble_sop(first, second) swapped, swapped_types = assemble_sop(second, first) assert Counter(ordered) == Counter(swapped) assert ordered != swapped and ordered_types != swapped_types assert len(ordered) == len(ordered_types) == 12 assert len(swapped) == len(swapped_types) == 12 sentence_order_labels = torch.tensor([0, 1]) sop_logits = torch.tensor([[math.log(3), 0.], [0., math.log(3)]], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True) sop_loss = F.cross_entropy(sop_logits, sentence_order_labels) assert math.isclose(sop_loss.item(), -math.log(.75)) sop_loss.backward() torch.testing.assert_close( sop_logits.grad, torch.tensor([[-.125, .125], [.125, -.125]], dtype=torch.float64) ) ``` The supplied logits assign probability 0.75 to the correct label in each row, giving mean loss about 0.28768. In training those scores would come from the shared encoder and sentence head; the derivative would reach both. SOP does not predict the next segment's words and does not turn the encoder into a document generator. For compatibility, the pinned preprocessor writes the label under the feature name `next_sentence_labels` even for SOP. It maps ordered to 0 and swapped to 1. It also retains a random-document fallback when a chunk contains only one segment. The ordered/swapped definition describes the intended two-segment task; exact preprocessing must also account for that fallback and truncation. [Lan et al., ALBERT v6, sections 3.1 and 4.6, Table 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.11942v6) compare three losses in an ALBERT-base configuration. The following are their reported measurements, not results of the small example: | Sentence loss | NSP accuracy, % | SOP accuracy, % | SQuAD 2.0 Dev F1 | RACE accuracy, % | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | none | 52.4 | 53.3 | 78.1 | 61.7 | | NSP | 90.5 | 52.0 | 77.2 | 62.3 | | SOP | 78.9 | 86.5 | 80.0 | 64.0 | High NSP accuracy did not transfer to the SOP diagnostic in this experiment. The downstream columns support the authors' choice for that setup; they do not prove that every NSP objective harms every model, or that solving reversed pairs establishes general discourse understanding. A useful diagnostic must test held-out documents and control for punctuation, segment length and other ordering cues. ## DeBERTa: разделить содержание и относительное положение

The predictions within the span are not fed to one another as decoder inputs; this remains encoder pretraining, not autoregressive generation of the missing phrase. The small module below checks the two read paths. It starts with supplied final encoder states rather than running another Transformer. Its widths are 4 for a state and 2 for an offset, not the original model dimensions. ```python import math import torch from torch import nn import torch.nn.functional as F torch.manual_seed(131) dtype = torch.float64 final_states = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(12, 4, dtype=dtype)) offsets = nn.Embedding(4, 2, dtype=dtype) vocabulary = nn.Embedding(12, 4, dtype=dtype) boundary_head = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(10, 8, bias=False, dtype=dtype), nn.GELU(), nn.LayerNorm(8, dtype=dtype), nn.Linear(8, 4, bias=False, dtype=dtype), nn.GELU(), nn.LayerNorm(4, dtype=dtype), ) # Zero-based rows 3 and 8 are h_4 and h_9 in the original figure. boundary_inputs = torch.cat([ final_states[3].expand(4, -1), final_states[8].expand(4, -1), offsets(torch.arange(4)), ], dim=-1) sbo_states = boundary_head(boundary_inputs) sbo_logits = F.linear(sbo_states, vocabulary.weight) mlm_logits = F.linear(final_states[4:8], vocabulary.weight) span_targets = torch.tensor([4, 5, 6, 7]) sbo_loss = F.cross_entropy(sbo_logits, span_targets) mlm_loss = F.cross_entropy(mlm_logits, span_targets) direct_sbo_gradient, = torch.autograd.grad( sbo_loss, final_states, retain_graph=True ) assert direct_sbo_gradient[3].norm() > 0 assert direct_sbo_gradient[8].norm() > 0 assert torch.count_nonzero(direct_sbo_gradient[4:8]) == 0 same_offset_inputs = boundary_inputs.clone() same_offset_inputs[:, -2:] = boundary_inputs[0, -2:] same_offset_logits = F.linear( boundary_head(same_offset_inputs), vocabulary.weight ) torch.testing.assert_close( same_offset_logits, same_offset_logits[0].expand_as(same_offset_logits) ) (mlm_loss + sbo_loss).backward() assert final_states.grad[4:8].norm() > 0 assert offsets.weight.grad.norm() > 0 assert vocabulary.weight.grad.norm() > 0 assert math.isclose(-math.log(.5) - math.log(.25), math.log(8)) ``` The zero internal-state derivative above concerns direct inputs to the SBO head at the final encoder output. In a complete encoder, the boundary states themselves depend on other positions through attention. SBO can therefore backpropagate through those earlier dependencies. The check does not say that all internal-position computations receive zero gradient throughout SpanBERT. ### Sampling several words without introducing a decoder Whole-word masking can select isolated words. SpanBERT instead starts from a word boundary and extends a contiguous span. Its proposed length distribution favors short spans but includes lengths up to ten words; the total target budget is about 15% of subword positions. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/bert-objectives-2026-10-29/spanbert-span-lengths.png|Original SpanBERT distribution of sampled span lengths]] *Joshi et al., [Figure 2, printed p. 66](https://aclanthology.org/2020.tacl-1.5.pdf#page=3), CC BY 4.0. Complete original plot and caption. The horizontal axis counts words, not WordPiece positions or decoder tokens.* In the released implementation, weights $0.2(0.8)^{\ell-1}$ for $\ell=1,\ldots,10$ are normalized over that finite range: $$ P(\ell)=\frac{0.2(0.8)^{\ell-1}}{1-0.8^{10}}, \qquad \ell\in\{1,\ldots,10\}. $$ This produces mean length about 3.8, as in the paper. Sampling an unbounded geometric variable and replacing every value above ten by ten would instead accumulate a tail probability at ten. That is a different distribution from the plotted and implemented one. ```python import math weights = [.2 * .8**(length - 1) for length in range(1, 11)] length_probabilities = [weight / sum(weights) for weight in weights] mean_words = sum(length * probability for length, probability in zip(range(1, 11), length_probabilities)) assert math.isclose(sum(length_probabilities), 1.) assert 3.79 < mean_words < 3.80 clamped_geometric_mean = sum(.8**step for step in range(10)) assert 4.46 < clamped_geometric_mean < 4.47 assert not math.isclose(mean_words, clamped_geometric_mean) ``` See [the pinned sampling code, lines 74–132](https://github.com/facebookresearch/SpanBERT/blob/0670d8b6a38f6714b85ea7a033f16bd8cc162676/pretraining/fairseq/data/masking.py#L74-L132). The paper describes spans of whole words; the released loop also stops at the exact subword budget, so its final selected word can be cut short. The sampled length distribution does not imply that every realized span has that many complete words after budget and document boundaries are applied. The original span-level replacement setting draws the corruption type once for a span: MASK, random replacements, or unchanged text. This differs from BERT's per-piece replacement loop. Adjacent selected intervals can also merge before SBO boundary targets are prepared. External boundaries must exist; the implementation does not fabricate a context token outside the document. The model also uses a single contiguous training segment without NSP. That input change and the auxiliary objective must be separated when reading results. In the paper's 1.2M-step ablation, Table 7 reports: | Span-masking setting | SQuAD 2.0 Dev F1 | NewsQA Dev F1 | Coreference F1 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | two segments + NSP | 85.4 | 73.0 | 76.4 | | one segment | 86.7 | 73.4 | 76.3 | | one segment + SBO | 86.8 | 74.1 | 79.0 | The first transition changes both the segment construction and NSP. The second keeps single-segment span masking and adds SBO. Its coreference gain is much larger than its SQuAD gain in this ablation. These are not the final 2.4M-step test results, and they do not establish one fixed improvement from adding SBO to any model. In [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/06 Encoder, Decoder и Encoder-Decoder/07 T5 — text-to-text Transformer|T5]], a deleted span is replaced by one sentinel and a separate causal decoder generates the missing text. SpanBERT retains the corrupted sequence's positions and predicts its selected tokens through encoder heads. The two methods share span-based corruption, but their target format, conditional dependencies and computation are different. ## ALBERT: classify the order of two document segments NSP's negative example can combine a paragraph about unlocking a door with a paragraph about penguins. A classifier can use the change of topic without learning which of two related events came first. ALBERT's sentence-order prediction (SOP) changes how the negative pair is built. Take consecutive segments from one document: | Label | First segment | Second segment | |---|---|---| | ordered | She unlocked the door. | Then she entered. | | swapped | Then she entered. | She unlocked the door. | Both rows contain the same words. A topic histogram of the combined text is identical, so that feature alone cannot distinguish these two labels. Token order, positions and segment membership do change. The segments need not be single linguistic sentences. The released ALBERT generator implements the swapped case as follows: ```python title="Original ALBERT pair swap — Apache-2.0" elif not FLAGS.random_next_sentence and rng.random() < 0.5: is_random_next = True for j in range(a_end, len(current_chunk)): tokens_b.extend(current_chunk[j]) # Note(mingdachen): in this case, we just swap tokens_a and tokens_b tokens_a, tokens_b = tokens_b, tokens_a ``` — Google Research, [create_pretraining_data.py, lines 338–343](https://github.com/google-research/albert/blob/b772393d3dae115b493258ce8e37c17b2cc62100/create_pretraining_data.py#L338-L343), Copyright 2019 The Google Research Authors, Apache-2.0. The historical variable name `is_random_next` also marks a swapped SOP pair; it does not mean that this branch sampled another document. Input assembly still produces `[CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP]`. The first segment and its initial special tokens receive type 0, the second segment and final separator type 1. Positional IDs run through the assembled sequence. The binary head reads the pooled `[CLS]` state, and its cross-entropy is added to MLM loss. The following calculation uses supplied logits to check target labels, mean cross-entropy and its gradient: ```python from collections import Counter import math import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def assemble_sop(first, second): tokens = ["[CLS]", *first, "[SEP]", *second, "[SEP]"] types = [0] * (len(first) + 2) + [1] * (len(second) + 1) return tokens, types first = ["she", "unlocked", "the", "door", "."] second = ["then", "she", "entered", "."] ordered, ordered_types = assemble_sop(first, second) swapped, swapped_types = assemble_sop(second, first) assert Counter(ordered) == Counter(swapped) assert ordered != swapped and ordered_types != swapped_types assert len(ordered) == len(ordered_types) == 12 assert len(swapped) == len(swapped_types) == 12 sentence_order_labels = torch.tensor([0, 1]) sop_logits = torch.tensor([[math.log(3), 0.], [0., math.log(3)]], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True) sop_loss = F.cross_entropy(sop_logits, sentence_order_labels) assert math.isclose(sop_loss.item(), -math.log(.75)) sop_loss.backward() torch.testing.assert_close( sop_logits.grad, torch.tensor([[-.125, .125], [.125, -.125]], dtype=torch.float64) ) ``` The supplied logits assign probability 0.75 to the correct label in each row, giving mean loss about 0.28768. In training those scores would come from the shared encoder and sentence head; the derivative would reach both. SOP does not predict the next segment's words and does not turn the encoder into a document generator. For compatibility, the pinned preprocessor writes the label under the feature name `next_sentence_labels` even for SOP. It maps ordered to 0 and swapped to 1. It also retains a random-document fallback when a chunk contains only one segment. The ordered/swapped definition describes the intended two-segment task; exact preprocessing must also account for that fallback and truncation. [Lan et al., ALBERT v6, sections 3.1 and 4.6, Table 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.11942v6) compare three losses in an ALBERT-base configuration. The following are their reported measurements, not results of the small example: | Sentence loss | NSP accuracy, % | SOP accuracy, % | SQuAD 2.0 Dev F1 | RACE accuracy, % | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | none | 52.4 | 53.3 | 78.1 | 61.7 | | NSP | 90.5 | 52.0 | 77.2 | 62.3 | | SOP | 78.9 | 86.5 | 80.0 | 64.0 | High NSP accuracy did not transfer to the SOP diagnostic in this experiment. The downstream columns support the authors' choice for that setup; they do not prove that every NSP objective harms every model, or that solving reversed pairs establishes general discourse understanding. A useful diagnostic must test held-out documents and control for punctuation, segment length and other ordering cues. ## DeBERTa: separate content from relative position
